comment: Authored OSCE scenarios. Numeric targets under 'derive' are placeholders filled from atlas label geometry by scripts/derive_osce_targets.py, which writes the merged web/osce.json. Edit THIS file, never web/osce.json.

scenarios.title: Lumbar radiculopathy
scenarios.stem: A 45-year-old presents with six weeks of left L5 radiculopathy: pain radiating below the knee into the dorsum of the foot, with a positive straight-leg raise. No fever, no history of malignancy, no trauma. The referral asks you to evaluate for lumbar disc herniation. Plan and acquire the exam.

feedback.pass: Sagittal T1 acquired. It shows marrow signal, vertebral alignment, and foraminal fat, the anatomic backbone of the study.
feedback.fail: The sagittal T1 was not acquired. Without it you lose marrow assessment and the fat planes that make foraminal narrowing visible.

feedback.pass: Sagittal T2 acquired. Disc hydration, canal caliber, and cord signal all read from this series.
feedback.fail: The sagittal T2 was not acquired. Disc desiccation, canal compromise, and cord signal cannot be assessed without it.

feedback.pass: Axial T2 acquired. The axial plane is where a posterolateral herniation and its relation to the traversing root are actually called.
feedback.fail: No axial T2 was acquired. A herniation's position (central, paracentral, foraminal) and root contact can only be judged in the axial plane.

feedback.pass: Contrast was correctly withheld. Gadolinium adds nothing for first-presentation radiculopathy without red flags.
feedback.fail: Post-contrast imaging was acquired. In first-presentation radiculopathy with no history of surgery, malignancy, or infection, gadolinium is not indicated. It is reserved for the postoperative spine (scar versus recurrent disc) and suspected tumor or infection.

criteria.label: Axial angled to the L4-L5 disc plane

feedback.pass: The axial stack is angled parallel to the L4-L5 disc. In-plane discs show the true canal and foraminal anatomy at the level that matters.
feedback.partial: The axial angulation is close but not parallel to the L4-L5 disc. Off-angle axials elongate the canal and can mimic or hide root compromise.
feedback.fail: The axial stack is not angled to the L4-L5 disc plane. Tilt the stack on the sagittal scout so slices run parallel to the disc; unangled axials cut the disc obliquely and distort the anatomy you are being asked to judge.

feedback.pass: The axial stack is centered on the L4-L5 disc, the level the clinical picture points to.
feedback.fail: The axial stack is not centered on L4-L5. A left L5 radiculopathy usually means L4-L5 disc pathology compressing the traversing L5 root, so center the stack there.

criteria.label: Axial coverage spans the lower three discs

feedback.pass: Axial coverage spans L3-L4 through L5-S1. If the symptomatic level is uncertain or there is pathology at an adjacent level, it is already covered.
feedback.partial: Axial coverage includes the L4-L5 disc but not the adjacent levels. The standard for radiculopathy is to cover the lower three discs, since an L5-S1 fragment can produce an identical picture.
feedback.fail: The axial slab does not cover the L4-L5 disc. Increase the slice count or thickness, or re-center the stack, so the symptomatic level is fully inside the coverage.

feedback.pass: Sagittal coverage extends across the full width of the discs, so both neural foramina are inside the stack.
feedback.partial: Sagittal coverage reaches most of the disc width but clips one side. A far-lateral herniation at the edge of coverage is exactly the lesion this exam exists to catch.
feedback.fail: The sagittal stack covers only the midline. Widen the stack so it extends through both neural foramina; foraminal and far-lateral herniations sit lateral to the canal.

feedback.pass: The STIR inversion time sits at the fat null. Marrow edema and soft-tissue fluid will be conspicuous against suppressed fat.
feedback.partial: The STIR inversion time is near the fat null but off enough to leave residual fat signal, which costs contrast for marrow edema.
feedback.fail: The STIR inversion time does not null fat. STIR works by inverting and then imaging at the moment fat crosses zero; at this TI fat still has signal and edema loses its conspicuity.

scenarios.title: Knee internal derangement
scenarios.stem: A 28-year-old basketball player felt a pop during a pivot, followed by swelling over hours and a sense of the knee giving way. Examination suggests a meniscal tear, with the cruciate ligaments to be assessed. Plan and acquire the exam.

feedback.pass: Coronal PD fat-sat acquired. Menisci and collateral ligaments read best in the coronal plane with fat suppressed.
feedback.fail: No coronal PD fat-sat was acquired. The body of each meniscus and the collateral ligaments are coronal-plane structures, and fat suppression is what makes their tears and the reactive edema conspicuous.

feedback.pass: Sagittal PD acquired. The anterior and posterior horns and the cruciates read in the sagittal plane.
feedback.fail: No sagittal PD was acquired. Meniscal horns and the ACL are judged on sagittal images; this is the workhorse series of a knee exam.

feedback.pass: Axial T2 fat-sat acquired. The patellofemoral compartment and retinacula are axial-plane reads, and the effusion is quantified here.
feedback.fail: No axial T2 fat-sat was acquired. The patellar cartilage, retinacula, and the effusion that follows an acute pivot injury are all assessed in the axial plane.

criteria.label: Non-fat-sat PD acquired for marrow and menisci detail

feedback.pass: A non-suppressed PD was acquired alongside the fat-sat series. Keeping one series without fat suppression preserves anatomic detail and marrow architecture.
feedback.fail: Every acquired series is fat-suppressed. Keeping one PD without fat suppression preserves meniscal and marrow detail that suppression trades away; the combination is the standard.

criteria.label: PD echo time stays proton-density weighted

feedback.pass: The echo time keeps the series proton-density weighted, where menisci retain enough signal for tears to appear as bright lines through dark fibrocartilage.
feedback.partial: The echo time is drifting toward T2 weighting. As TE grows, meniscal signal drops and subtle tears lose their conspicuity.
feedback.fail: At this echo time the series is T2 weighted, not proton density. The meniscus goes uniformly dark on long TE images and intrasubstance tears disappear into it.

feedback.pass: Sagittal coverage spans the cartilage from compartment to compartment, so both menisci are fully inside the stack.
feedback.partial: Sagittal coverage reaches most of the joint but clips a compartment edge. The peripheral third of the meniscus at the edge of coverage is a common tear site.
feedback.fail: The sagittal stack covers only the central joint. Widen the coverage so both femorotibial compartments are included from edge to edge.

scenarios.title: Brain, first seizure
scenarios.stem: A 31-year-old had a first generalized seizure witnessed at home, with full recovery and a normal neurological examination. There is no fever, trauma, malignancy history, or immunocompromise. The referral asks for a seizure-protocol MRI. Plan and acquire the exam.

feedback.pass: FLAIR acquired. With CSF nulled, cortical and periventricular lesions such as mesial temporal sclerosis or cortical dysplasia stand out; this is the single highest-yield sequence for epilepsy.
feedback.fail: FLAIR was not acquired. On plain T2 a periventricular or cortical lesion sits next to bright CSF and can vanish into it; nulling the CSF is what makes the classic epileptogenic lesions visible.

feedback.pass: T1 acquired, giving the anatomic reference and gray-white differentiation for the study.
feedback.fail: No T1 was acquired. Gray-white differentiation and anatomy assessment need a T1 series.

feedback.pass: T2 acquired. Most parenchymal pathology is T2 bright, and it pairs with FLAIR to separate true lesions from CSF-space artifact.
feedback.fail: No T2 was acquired. FLAIR alone is not enough; T2 confirms lesions and shows posterior fossa detail where FLAIR is weakest.

feedback.pass: Diffusion acquired. A first seizure can be the presentation of an acute infarct, and postictal changes have a diffusion signature too.
feedback.fail: No diffusion was acquired. An acute infarct can present as a first seizure, and DWI is the only sequence that reliably shows it in the first hours.

feedback.pass: Contrast was correctly withheld. With a normal examination and no red flags, the non-contrast seizure protocol is the appropriate first study.
feedback.fail: Post-contrast imaging was acquired. In a first unprovoked seizure with full recovery and a normal examination, gadolinium is reserved for cases where the non-contrast study finds a lesion or the history suggests tumor or infection.

feedback.pass: The inversion time sits at the CSF null, which is the entire point of FLAIR: dark ventricles and sulci with lesions left bright.
feedback.partial: The inversion time is near the CSF null but off enough that CSF keeps some signal, which erodes the contrast that makes periventricular lesions visible.
feedback.fail: At this inversion time CSF is not nulled and the sequence no longer behaves as FLAIR. The TI must sit where the CSF longitudinal recovery crosses zero for this TR.

criteria.label: Diffusion b-value in the stroke range

feedback.pass: The b-value sits in the standard stroke range near 1000, enough diffusion weighting to make restriction conspicuous without starving the image of signal.
feedback.partial: The b-value is outside the usual stroke range. Very low values leave T2 shine-through dominant, very high values cost SNR that small cortical infarcts need.
feedback.fail: At this b-value the series is not diagnostically diffusion weighted for stroke. Restriction contrast needs b near 1000.
